entities.label: Aztec, New Mexico crash claim, March 1948
entities.sub: A retrieval story with no retrieval behind it: the documented history is a Denver oil-fraud scheme
entities.locLabel: Hart Canyon, near Aztec, San Juan County, New Mexico
entities.desc:
Aztec is on this board for one reason, and it is not that a saucer came down in Hart Canyon. It is the earliest fully traceable example of a crash-retrieval narrative whose entire provenance can be reconstructed end to end - source, motive, transmission, monetisation, exposure, conviction, and revival - and that makes it the control case against which every other retrieval claim on this board has to be measured. Everything the story needed to survive it had: named military witnesses, a specific canyon, a specific craft diameter, a specific body count, a bestselling book, a metal sample, and a federal-sounding cover-up. What it did not have was a crash.

The chain begins with Silas Mason Newton, a Denver oil promoter whose name first reached the FBI on 24 September 1938 on a suspected wire-fraud referral, and Leo (Leonard) A. GeBauer, a Phoenix electronics merchant who appears in the literature under the pseudonym 'Dr. Gee', the 'magnetologist'. On 8 March 1950 Newton, billed only as 'Mr. X' or 'Scientist X', lectured a room of science students at the University of Denver. He told them he had seen two recovered flying saucers held in a secret government facility; one had come down near Aztec, New Mexico, brought down by a 'magnetic fault line', the other near Durango, Colorado. The occupants of the first had been burned dark brown when a porthole blew out; the crew of the second had suffocated from a change in atmosphere. He described the beings as between 38 and 42 inches tall, dressed in cloth that could not be torn, probably from Venus, flying on magnetic propulsion at twice the speed of light.

Frank Scully, a Variety columnist, had already begun retailing the story in his 1949 columns. In 1950 Henry Holt published 'Behind the Flying Saucers', which turned Newton's lecture into a bestseller and into the template. Scully's version put the event in March 1948, a 99-foot craft - the largest UFO reported to that date - containing sixteen humanoid bodies, recovered by the military after a controlled landing in Hart Canyon roughly twelve miles northeast of Aztec, and hauled away for secret research. Scully added that the craft ran on 'magnetic principles', that the crew carried concentrated food wafers and heavy water, and that every dimension of the vehicle was divisible by nine. Martin Gardner, in 'Fads and Fallacies in the Name of Science', took the book apart as 'wild imaginings' and 'scientific howlers'.

The monetisation is the part that matters. Through the late 1940s and early 1950s Newton and GeBauer were travelling the Four Corners selling 'doodlebugs' - devices that in the oil business claim to locate deposits by remote sensing - and their sales pitch was that the doodlebug was built from, or reverse-engineered out of, the alien technology recovered at Aztec. Herman A. Flader, a Denver industrialist, put in $50,000 for a partnership in GeBauer's Colorado Geophysics & Development company, on the represented understanding that each unit cost around $800,000 to build. Dr. Alfred D. Kleyhauer, a Denver optometrist, lost $15,000. When investigators opened the devices they found surplus military radio parts; the estimated build cost was about $3.50 each. When J. P. Cahn of the San Francisco Chronicle demanded a sample of the miracle metal, the sample tested as ordinary aluminium. Cahn published the exposure in True magazine in September 1952 and returned in August 1956 with a second piece cataloguing further victims. Flader pressed charges. Newton and GeBauer were convicted of fraud in 1953 and also faced federal charges for moving the proceeds across state lines. Neither did jail time; the Denver Public Library's account records Newton still on probation and in violation of its terms by June 1955, and on 30 April 1969 he pleaded guilty again, this time to salting the Buckhorn Mine at Silver City, New Mexico. He died in 1972, probably still on probation.

The story should have died in 1956 and did, for about fifteen years - through the mid-1950s to the early 1970s most ufologists treated it as radioactive. It came back because the surrounding mythology gave it somewhere to live. In 1974 Robert Spencer Carr publicly claimed alien bodies recovered near Aztec were held at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, drawing official Air Force denials. Leonard Stringfield in the late 1970s went further, arguing the craft was one of many the US military had captured and stored. From there the Aztec details - the small burned bodies, the intact hull, the fast military sanitisation of the site - migrated wholesale into later allegedly first-hand accounts of Roswell, which is the single most important structural fact in this dossier: a documented hoax became a donor of detail to the case that the modern disclosure argument rests on.

It also acquired a paper artefact that will not go away. On 22 March 1950, two weeks after Newton's Denver lecture, Guy Hottel, special agent in charge of the FBI's Washington Field Office, filed a one-page memo relaying a third-party account of three recovered circular craft in New Mexico, 'approximately 50 feet in diameter', each holding three bodies 'only three feet tall' in 'metallic cloth', allegedly downed by high-powered radar. The memo ends 'No further evaluation was attempted'. When the FBI launched The Vault in April 2011 the Hottel memo became its most-viewed document, and in March 2013 the Bureau published a statement that it 'does not prove the existence of UFOs; it is simply a second- or third-hand claim that we never investigated', adding that some believe it simply repeats a hoax then in circulation.

Revisionism continues. Aztec's public library ran an annual UFO Symposium as a library fundraiser from 1997 to 2011. Scott and Suzanne Ramsey, with journalism professor Frank Thayer, spent three decades on the case and published 'The Aztec Incident: Recovery at Hart Canyon' (2012) and 'The Aztec UFO Incident' (2016), arguing the crash was real and independently witnessed; Ramsey placed a commemorative plaque at the canyon site in 2007. Nothing in that body of work has displaced the trial record. Tier it accordingly: the fraud is documented, the retrieval is not.

openQuestions: The exact sentence imposed in 1953 is not established from a primary court record. The Denver Public Library article states the specific sentence 'appears to be lost to time'; a reader comment on that article cites Denver Post 14 June 1954 p.3 and Rocky Mountain News 15 June 1954 p.10 for no jail time, five years probation, costs and restitution. That microfilm has not been checked here and the sentence detail is therefore unverified.
Scully's 1949 Variety columns have not been read in the original; the 1949 date rests on secondary sources.
The Ramsey/Thayer witness roster has not been independently examined. No claim in this dossier rests on it.

entities.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés (CNES)
entities.sub: France has run a state UAP office inside its space agency continuously since 1977 and publishes the case files
entities.locLabel: CNES Centre Spatial de Toulouse, France
entities.desc:
GEIPAN is the answer to the question the US posture keeps deflecting: what does it actually look like when a government decides that unidentified aerospace phenomena are a normal object of public administration. The answer is a two- or three-person office in a space agency, a volunteer investigator corps, a steering committee of police, gendarmes, air force, meteorologists and scientists, a published four-tier classification, and a searchable public archive of every closed case. It has run without interruption since 1977 under three names.

CNES states plainly on its own site that it has studied unidentified aerospace phenomena since 1977, the year GEPAN - the Groupe d'Étude des Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés - was created. Its origin was not a scandal or a leak but a recommendation: a 1976 Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale committee, chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, opened the UFO file with the explicit objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection, and GEPAN was created on the back of that committee's recommendations. That lineage is stated in the COMETA report's own introduction. Claude Poher directed GEPAN at its inception. In 1988 GEPAN was replaced by SEPRA, the Service d'Études des Phénomènes de Rentrées Atmosphériques, which absorbed the UAP function into a unit whose principal job was routine monitoring of orbital debris and re-entry risk objects. At the end of 2001 the CNES Direction Générale commissioned an audit to decide the activity's future. The 2005 outcome was restructuring rather than closure: GEIPAN replaced SEPRA, and the audit carried what CNES calls 'une recommandation importante d'informer le public en toute transparence' - an important recommendation to inform the public in complete transparency. That recommendation is embedded in the acronym; the added 'I' stands for Information. It was implemented starting in 2007 with the online publication of GEIPAN's archives and case files.

The structure is worth stating precisely because it is the operational counter-model. GEIPAN sits under the deputy directorate of the Toulouse Space Centre. It is steered by a comité de pilotage (COPEIPAN) chaired by a recognised figure from the aerospace world and composed of representatives of the country's civil and military authorities - Gendarmerie nationale, civil aviation, meteorology, the Air and Space Force, scientific research - plus CNES. That committee's job is to analyse GEIPAN's results and make recommendations to CNES on its direction. Beneath it sits a collège d'experts of roughly thirty multidisciplinary volunteers who take the hardest cases, and a corps of volunteer field investigators across France who are mandated case by case and work to the methods set out in GEIPAN's investigator guide. GEIPAN holds standing conventions with the Gendarmerie, the Air Force, civil aviation, the Navy and Météo France for rapid access to hard data, and works with CNRS and the CEA. The permanent staff, per GEIPAN's own history page, is two full-time CNES agents - the head and an assistant - supported by external contractors for case analysis, statistics, anonymisation and archiving. Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor, surveying the office in 2025, counted three full-time employees and over 20 trained volunteer investigators. Funding comes out of the general public-service subsidy CNES receives; there is no separate UAP line item. Frederic Courtade has headed GEIPAN since January 2024.

The classification is what makes the archive usable. Each case is scored on two axes - consistency (C), the product of the quantity and reliability of data, and residual strangeness (E) after comparison against known-phenomenon hypotheses - then filed as A (perfectly identified), B (probably identified), C (unidentified for lack of data) or D (unidentified after investigation). Cases in C and D can be reopened if new information arrives. As of the site statistics dated 11 August 2026, 3,381 published classified cases break down as 950 class A (28.1%), 1,310 class B (38.7%), 1,015 class C (30.0%) and 106 class D (3.1%). Canada's report, working from the 2025 figures, recorded 3,188 cases with 3.2% unidentified after investigation and 31.4% unexplained for insufficient data. The residual is small, it is stable, and it is public.

GEIPAN is also unusually explicit about what it is not. Its FAQ states that it is not an independent structure but a technical department of CNES; that it carries no national-security, space-surveillance or alert mission; and that, 'contrary to popular belief', it is not a research group on UFOs, extraterrestrial life or other paranormal phenomena. It uses only recognised scientific knowledge, 'without speculation or unverified hypotheses'. That disclaimer is not evasion - it is the price of the archive, and it is precisely the trade the US system has refused to make.

The substantive work is on the record. In June 1978 GEPAN presented its scientific council with a five-volume, roughly 500-page report on the first semester of 1978; a contemporaneous English-language summary of that report, held in the NSA's public UFO document collection, records that eleven high-credibility, high-strangeness cases were studied in detail, that only one proved to have a conventional explanation, that in ten of the eleven the conclusion was that witnesses had seen a material phenomenon explicable as neither a natural phenomenon nor a human device, and that the report concluded there was behind the phenomenon a 'flying machine. . . whose modes of sustenance and propulsion are beyond our knowledge'. The same summary judges that the care taken with distances, angles and psychological factors 'makes the bulk of the Condon Report seem very poor by comparison'. GEPAN's most cited physical-trace investigation, the Trans-en-Provence landing of 8 January 1981, was published as Note Technique n° 16, 'Analyse d'une trace', issued by CNES in Toulouse on 1 March 1983 and still hosted on the GEIPAN site.

The office's standing outside France is the argument in compressed form. When Canada's Chief Science Advisor set out to design a national UAP reporting system in 2025, GEIPAN was the model it described in the most detail, the example it explicitly told Canada to consider when establishing a dedicated service, and one of only four international bodies - alongside AARO, NASA and Chile's SEFAA - that it recommended Canada partner with.

'Fin 2001, la Direction générale du CNES commande un audit pour statuer sur l'avenir de l'activité. CNES lists GEIPAN's inception as 1977, its location as CNES Toulouse, its lifetime as 'Indefinite' and its status as 'In operation', with partners Gendarmerie, Police, Air and Space Force, CNRS and Meteo France; 'Currently headed by Frédéric Courtade since January 2024, GEIPAN is overseen by COPEIPAN, a steering committee'.

Key milestones per CNES: '2008: GEIPAN website created and UAP archives transferred to it; 2005: GEIPAN replaces SEPRA; 1988: GEPAN replaced by SEPRA, the permanent unit at CNES responsible for routine monitoring of orbital debris and risk objects; 1977: Inception of GEPAN'.

'In 10 of the 11 cases, the conclusion was that the witnesses had witnessed a material phenomenon that could not be explained as a natural phenomenon or a human device', and the report concluded that behind the phenomenon there is a 'flying machine. . . whose modes of sustenance and propulsion are beyond our knowledge'.

Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor: 'France's GEIPAN ... operates under the French space agency CNES ... since 1977. Its mission is to collect, investigate and archive UAP reports, and make its findings available to the public.' It records 'of the 3,188 cases collected by 2025, only 3.2% of cases remained unidentified after investigation. Furthermore, 31.4% of cases could not be explained due to insufficient data.'

claims.text: The same report records that GEIPAN has 'a team of three full-time employees', that reports are investigated by 'over 20 trained volunteers throughout France', and that its guiding principles include 'low operational costs, public service, respect for witnesses and a commitment to transparency, neutrality and objective investigation'.

openQuestions: GEIPAN's own history page states a permanent team of two full-time CNES agents; Canada's 2025 report states three full-time employees. Both are cited above. The discrepancy is unresolved and may simply reflect a headcount change between the two publication dates.
GEIPAN's annual budget is not published as a separate figure; CNES states only that it comes out of the general public-service subsidy. No euro figure has been sourced.
The full text of the 2001-2005 CNES audit that produced the restructuring and the transparency recommendation has not been located online.

entities.label: COMETA report, 'Les OVNI et la Défense: à quoi doit-on se préparer?' (July 1999)
entities.sub: Retired French generals, admirals and IHEDN auditors put the defence question in writing and named the extraterrestrial hypothesis
entities.desc:
COMETA is the document that has no American equivalent. A committee of retired French flag officers - an air force general in the chair, a vice-admiral, a weapons engineer general, a chief of police from the Interior Ministry, a research director from ONERA - spent close to three years reviewing UAP case material, wrote ninety pages under the title 'UFOs and Defense: What Should We Prepare For?', concluded that the extraterrestrial hypothesis could not be excluded and was the most credible of the available explanations, and put their names on it. It was not commissioned by the French state, and its authors are careful about that. But it was written by people the French state had trained to think about national defence, using material from the French state's own UAP office, and it reads as a defence staff study rather than a polemic.

The committee's institutional centre of gravity is the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale. Almost every named member is an IHEDN auditor, identified by promotion number: Michel Algrin, doctor of political science and attorney-at-law (AA 35); Pierre Bescond, Weapons Engineer General, 2nd Section (AA 48); Denis Blancher, Chief of Police, Police Nationale, Ministry of the Interior; Jean Dunglas, honorary engineer general (AR 48); Bruno Le Moine, Air Force General, 2nd Section (AA 41); Françoise Lepine of the Fondation pour les Études de Défense (AA 33); Christian Marchal, research director at ONERA; Marc Merlo, Admiral, 2nd Section (AA 35); and Alain Orszag, Weapons Engineer General, 2nd Section. General Denis Letty, Air Force, 2nd Section (AA 35), chaired it. The report carries a foreword by Professor André Lebeau, former chairman of CNES, and one by General Bernard Norlain, former director of IHEDN, whom Letty visited at IHEDN in March 1995 to explain the project. Letty thanks both, saying that without them 'COMETA would not have been born'.

The report's own account of its lineage matters for this board because it closes a loop back to GEIPAN. COMETA's introduction states that in 1976 an IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale opened the unidentified flying objects file with the objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection, that 'the goal was achieved, because the recommendations of this committee were followed in the creation of' GEPAN, and that twenty years later it seemed useful to take stock again. In other words the same institution produced both the French state's UAP office and, two decades on, the committee that reviewed its output.

The evidentiary base is the French official record. Contributors included Jean-Jacques Velasco, then head of SEPRA at CNES; François Louange, chief executive of the image-analysis firm Fleximage; the pilots Jean-Charles Duboc, Jean-Pierre Fartek and René Giraud; Edmond Campagnac, former technical director of Air France at Antananarivo; Squadron Commander Michel Perrier of the Gendarmerie Nationale; an official of the DGAC; and Air Force General Joseph Domange. Letty specifically thanks the commander of the Air Force Air Operations Command Center for its participation in the investigation into Air France flight AF 3532 of 28 January 1994.

On substance, COMETA reproduces GEPAN/SEPRA's four-category scheme and then states the number that the whole document turns on: 'Category D UAPs represent 4 to 5% of the cases and are called UAP Ds.' Category D means unidentified despite the abundance and quality of the data - not unidentified for want of it. The report's position is that a residue of that size, often attested by consistent testimony and by visual sightings coupled with radar, can no longer be filed as no action: 'if there had only been ten or so UAP D [sightings], this ambiguous file could just have been classified as "no action," but we are no longer at that point and are far beyond that. Thus we are forced to seek plausible explanations.' It records around one hundred GEPAN/SEPRA investigations, several of which 'demonstrated, in the end, the physical presence of a phenomenon the nature and origin of which remain unknown', singling out Trans-en-Provence (8 January 1981) and 'Amaranth' (21 October 1982), documented in GEPAN technical memoranda 16 and 17. On aeronautical cases it records twelve French cases, only three or four of them category D; the first, in 1951, involving Vampire aircraft near Orange; and AF 3532 on 28 January 1994 as the first French case of a visual sighting correlated with radar over fifty seconds. It also draws on Dominique Weinstein's enumeration of 489 well-documented aeronautical UAP D cases worldwide since 1942, most from official sources.

COMETA is structured in three parts - facts and testimonies, the extent of current knowledge, and UFOs and defence - plus a conclusion and seven appendices, among them 'Radar Detection in France', 'Life in the Universe', 'Colonization of Space' and 'The Roswell Affair - Disinformation'. Its recommendations are set out in the introduction: give civilian and military pilots enough information to adopt adapted conduct when faced with these phenomena, and inform the public and decision-makers more generally; develop the actions of SEPRA and promote supplemental scientific monitoring and research; and consider the strategic, political and religious consequences of a possible confirmation of the extraterrestrial hypothesis, 'the bizarre connotation of which it is advisable to eliminate here and now'. Letty's own framing, in the foreword, is the sentence most often quoted from the document and is verbatim: 'The accumulation of well-documented sightings made by credible witnesses forces us to consider from now on all of the hypotheses regarding the origin of unidentified flying objects, or UFOs, and the extraterrestrial hypothesis, in particular.'

COMETA the association was registered under the French law of 1901 on 24 February 1999, having operated informally since 1996, and went dormant around 2006. The report appeared in July 1999 in a special issue of VSD, was reissued by Éditions du Rocher in 2003, and was not widely circulated in its original form because of copyright restrictions. According to Robert Roussel, citing Olivier Schrameck, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin read and annotated it 'to mark his interest'. There was no formal government response beyond that. GEIPAN made an archive of the report public in 2007.

claims.text: Introduction, verbatim: 'In 1976, a committee of the Institut des Hautes Etudes de Defense Nationale (IHEDN) chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale opened the unidentified flying objects file. The objective: to make proposals for organizing research and the collection of data on these phenomena. The goal was achieved, because the recommendations of this committee were followed in the creation of the Groupe d'Etude des Phenomenes Aerospatiaux Non Identifies (GEPAN).'

Chapter 7.2, verbatim: 'Category D UAPs represent 4 to 5% of the cases and are called UAP Ds', where category D is 'phenomenon that cannot be identified despite the abundance and quality of the data'.

Chapter 8.3, verbatim: 'if there had only been ten or so UAP D [sightings], this ambiguous file could just have been classified as "no action," but we are no longer at that point and are far beyond that. Thus we are forced to seek plausible explanations.'

Chapter 7.4: 'Around one hundred investigations have been conducted by GEPAN/SEPRA'; several 'demonstrated, in the end, the physical presence of a phenomenon the nature and origin of which remain unknown', naming Trans-en-Provence (8 January 1981) and 'Amaranth' (21 October 1982), 'detailed in GEPAN technical memoranda no. 16 and no. 17'.

Chapter 7.5: twelve French aeronautical cases were known to GEPAN/SEPRA, 'only three or four of these can be considered to fall into category D'; the first UAP D dates to 1951 involving Vampire military aircraft near Orange; and not until 28 January 1994 did an Air France crew produce 'the first case of a visual sighting correlated with a radar detection over 50 seconds long'. A worldwide list compiled by Dominique Weinstein describes '489 well-documented cases of aeronautical UAP D sightings the sources of which were duly verified'.

Recommendations stated in the introduction: provide civilian and military pilots with sufficient information and adapted conduct, and the public and decision-makers with information; 'developing the actions of SEPRA and promoting supplemental scientific monitoring, or even research, actions'; and 'considering the strategic, political, and religious consequences of a possible confirmation of the extraterrestrial hypothesis, the bizarre connotation of which it is advisable to eliminate here and now.'

Structure: three parts and a conclusion, with Part 3 titled 'UFOs and Defense' and seven appendices including 'Radar Detection in France', 'Astronomers' Sightings', 'Life in the Universe', 'Colonization of Space' and 'The Roswell Affair -Disinformation'.

COMETA 'operated informally since 1996' and 'was officially registered as a non-profit association under the French law of 1901 on February 24, 1999'; it became dormant around 2006, and the report 'was not widely circulated due to copyright restrictions'. It was reissued in book form by Éditions du Rocher in 2003 (ISBN 2-268-04592-7), and an archive was made public in 2007 by GEIPAN.
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COMETA_report, citing Kragel & Couprie, 'OVNIS, Enquête sur un secret d'état' (Cherche Midi, 2010) and Rossoni, 'Les OVNI du CNES' (2005)

claims.text: According to Olivier Schrameck, chief of staff to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, Jospin read and annotated the COMETA report 'to mark his interest' on receiving it; the French government made no official response beyond that.
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COMETA_report, citing Robert Roussel, 'Ovnis 1947-2017. Le choix du déni' (L'Harmattan, 2018), p. 214

openQuestions: The English-language PDF used here appears to be truncated at approximately page 40, ending inside chapter 8.3.6. The full 'Conclusion and Recommendations' section listed in the table of contents was not readable in this copy, so the frequently quoted conclusion about an 'almost certain physical reality' of unknown craft has deliberately NOT been quoted or attributed here.

Whether COMETA was formally transmitted to President Jacques Chirac, and by what route, is not established from any primary source located. Several secondary accounts assert it; the English Wikipedia flags the Velasco-to-Jospin handover as uncited.
The original French first edition (VSD hors-série, July 1999) has not been consulted; all verbatim quotations above are from the English translation.
sources: COMETA, 'Les OVNI et la Défense - À quoi doit-on se préparer ?', Éditions du Rocher, 2003, ISBN 2-268-04592-7

entities.label: CEFAA / SEFAA - Chile's anomalous aerial phenomena office, Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
entities.sub: A civil aviation regulator that has treated UAP as a flight-safety problem, on the record, since 1997
entities.locLabel: Santiago, Chile (Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica, Quinta Normal, 1997-2009; Cerrillos, Santiago, current)
entities.desc:
Chile's UAP office exists because pilots kept reporting things and a civil aviation authority decided that was an aviation-safety matter rather than an embarrassment. That framing - not disclosure, not exobiology, but the safety of air operations in 32 million square kilometres of airspace - is what has kept it alive for nearly thirty years and what makes it the South American counterweight on this board.

The prehistory runs back to 1968. Anomalous aerial phenomena were first reported officially in Chile at the old Oficina Meteorológica de Chile in the Quinta Normal aeronautical complex in Santiago, where the director, Aviation Colonel Sergio Bravo Flores, began collecting reports and led the Comisión Chilena para Estudios de Fenómenos Espaciales No Identificados, formed with the support of the Sociedad Científica de Chile. Bravo's first act, on 9 July 1968, was to circulate 43 aeronautical installations from Arica to the Chilean Antarctic asking for reports. The commission - a meteorologist from Línea Aérea Nacional, an engineer, a physician, a doctor of physical and mathematical sciences, a Chilean Air Force lieutenant seconded to the aeronautics directorate, and several engineers - stated its object as establishing 'with all seriousness the true causes' of the matter. In seven years it gathered around a dozen reports, some of which were forwarded to the University of Colorado, where the panel later known as the Condon Committee was at work. It wound up in 1975 when Bravo retired.

The modern office was created twenty-two years later. A wave of sightings reported over Arica in the last days of March and first days of April 1997, together with the expressed interest of the former Commander-in-Chief of the Chilean Air Force, General del Aire Ramón Vega Hidalgo, moved the Director General of Civil Aeronautics, Aviation General Gonzalo Miranda Aguirre, to create the Comité de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos on 3 October 1997, by Resolución Exenta N° 01599. The resolution sited the committee at the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in Quinta Normal, Santiago, and on 14 October 1997 the school's director, Colonel Enzo Di Nocera García, set out its organisation and operating basis and named its members: himself as head, air traffic controller Gustavo Rodríguez Navarro, and the heads of the air traffic and meteorology areas as consultants, with ETA specialists and external organisations convened as needed. In practice Rodríguez Navarro carried the office's work through its early years.

The institutional history is not a straight line, and the dossier is stronger for saying so. Di Nocera led the committee until 1998, when Air Brigade General Ricardo Bermúdez Sanhueza took over the ETA and with it CEFAA, running it to February 2002. Air Brigade General Hernán Henríquez Cobaise took the directorship in March 2002 and held it to 31 March 2008, and the DGAC's own account describes the period from March 2002 to March 2008 as 'una etapa de latencia' - a dormancy. On 15 December 2009, by Resolución N° 02/0/01937, Director General José Huepe Pérez ordered the committee to operate from 1 January 2010 reporting directly to the Secretaría General, detaching it from the ETA and putting its members on permanent, exclusively investigative postings. Bermúdez returned to the directorship in 2009 and served to 2016; Hugo Camus Palacios succeeded him. On 18 October 2021, Resolución Exenta N° 04/3/0113/1385 repealed the 1997 resolution and renamed the office the Sección de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos, moving it under the DGAC's Subdepartamento Comunicacional. It is now based at Av. Pedro Aguirre Cerda 5100, Cerrillos, Santiago.

Its remit is defined by airspace, not by belief. SEFAA's mission is to support the safety of air operations in the national territory and in the airspace of DGAC responsibility, which extends across 32 million square kilometres from Arica in the north, between 120° and 131° west, to the South Pole. Its principal source is pilot reports - military, commercial, private, sport and institutional - supplemented by public reports, and it explicitly reserves the right to select which material is investigable. Investigations are grounded in the scientific method and depend heavily on audiovisual records. A digital case database was created in 2018; by September 2021 the office had received 1,675 cases in total, with 362 arriving in 2020 alone, nearly a 300% jump on prior years, and 300 more by September 2021. Since 2020 investigated and resolved cases have been published on the office's website, with reports made available to the public quarterly, and resolved-case pages remain live by year through 2026. The permanent staff is small - in 2018 the committee comprised its director and two investigators - but it draws on an external research committee of astronomers, geographers, physicists, psychologists, a nuclear chemist, aerospace medicine specialists, air traffic controllers, a meteorologist, aeronautical investigators, inspector pilots, aeronautical engineers, image analysts and armed forces representatives. On its 24th anniversary the DGAC described CEFAA as 'uno de los organismos públicos más antiguos del continente' and as leading a transparency model comparable, allowing for the difference in human and budgetary resources, to a European government body.

Its most visible case is the Chilean Navy footage of 11 November 2014, in which an Airbus Cougar AS-532 helicopter crew recorded roughly ten minutes of infrared video of an object off the coast west of Santiago. CEFAA investigated for over two years and released the footage with an official report in January 2017; Bermúdez, who had directed the investigation, summarised the outcome as knowing what it was not rather than what it was. The case is also the clearest documented instance of European-South American technical cooperation on UAP: photo and video analysts in France, including François Louange, were brought in through GEIPAN, and GEIPAN's analysts proposed a mundane explanation - a medium-haul aircraft venting - that CEFAA rejected. Independent analysts subsequently matched the timestamps and geometry to scheduled flights. The disagreement is the point: two state UAP offices on different continents worked the same tape, reached different conclusions, and both published.

That visibility is now institutional. Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor, designing a national UAP reporting system in 2025, described SEFAA as one of only three national models worth examining alongside the United States and France, and recommended that Canada's lead organisation establish partnerships with AARO and NASA, GEIPAN and SEFAA.

claims.text: 'El 3 de octubre de 1997 se creó el Comité de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos (CEFAA), a través de la Resolución Exenta N° 01599. Sin embargo, el 18 de octubre de 2021 la mencionada Resolución fue derogada, y por Resolución Exenta N° 04 / 3 / 0113 / 1385 el nombre de la oficina fue cambiado a Sección de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos (SEFAA), pasando a depender del Subdepartamento Comunicacional de la DGAC.'

The creating resolution was 'firmada por el Director General de Aeronáutica Civil, General de Aviación, Gonzalo Miranda', and sited the committee at the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in Quinta Normal, Santiago; on 14 October 1997 ETA director Enzo Di Nocera 'estableció la organización y las bases de su funcionamiento' and named its members.

The creation was prompted by 'una serie de avistamientos reportados en la ciudad de Arica en los últimos días de marzo y primeros de abril de 1997' together with 'el interés manifestado por el ex Comandante en Jefe de la Fuerza Aérea de Chile, General del Aire Ramón Vega Hidalgo'.

Predecessor body: from 1968 Aviation Colonel Sergio Bravo Flores, director of the Oficina Meteorológica de Chile, led the Comisión Chilena para Estudios de Fenómenos Espaciales No Identificados, formed with support of the Sociedad Científica de Chile. On 9 July 1968 he circulated 43 aeronautical installations requesting reports; the commission ran to 1975 and some of its dozen or so reports were sent to the University of Colorado, 'en donde la una comisión de académicos (bautizada posteriormente como Comisión Condon) realizaba un detallado estudio'.

Directorship chronology per DGAC: Di Nocera to 1998; Ricardo Bermúdez 1998 to February 2002; Hernán Henríquez Cobaise from March 2002 to 31 March 2008, during which period 'el CEFAA entró en una etapa de latencia'; reactivated by Resolución N° 02/0/01937 of 15 December 2009 under Director General José Huepe Pérez, operating from 1 January 2010 under the Secretaría General; Bermúdez again from 2009 to 2016; then Hugo Camus Palacios.

Remit: 'Apoyar la seguridad de las operaciones aéreas en el territorio nacional, y en el espacio aéreo de responsabilidad de la Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil de Chile', an airspace that 'se extiende por 32 millones de kilómetros cuadrados, desde Arica, por el norte, entre los 120º y los 131º grados oeste, hasta el Polo Sur.'

Caseload as of September 2021: 'ha recepcionado un total de 1675 casos'; 'El año 2020 llegaron 362 casos, superando en casi un 300% las cifras que se venían registrando en años anteriores'; 300 further reports to September 2021; supported by 'una Base de Datos Digital creada el año 2018'.

Publication practice: 'Desde el año 2020, se publican en el sitio www.cefaa.gob.cl los casos investigados y resueltos. Esos informes están a disposición del público trimestralmente y entregan una completa descripción de los fenómenos reportados y la conclusión a la que se llegó.' Resolved-case indexes remain published by year from 2018 through 2026.

On its 24th anniversary the DGAC described CEFAA as 'uno de los organismos públicos más antiguos del continente' and stated that, 'Comparable a un organismo gubernamental europeo -guardando las proporciones en cuanto a recursos humanos y presupuestarios- el CEFAA lidera un modelo de transparencia respecto a sus investigaciones.'

As of October 2018 CEFAA comprised 'su Director, Hugo Camus Palacios y dos investigadores', supported by an external research committee of astronomers, geographers, physicists, psychologists, a nuclear chemist, aerospace medicine professionals, air traffic controllers, a meteorologist, aeronautical investigators, inspector pilots, aeronautical engineers, image analysts and armed forces representatives.

Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor: 'In Chile, the SEFAA ... serves as the official body responsible for collecting, analyzing and scientifically studying UAPs. It operates within the General Directorate of Civil Aeronautics.' It adds that 'SEFAA publishes monthly reports detailing the cases it has received, investigated, and closed'.

The Chilean Navy case: an Airbus Cougar AS-532 helicopter with an infrared camera recorded roughly ten minutes of footage of an unidentified object off the coast west of Santiago on 11 November 2014; CEFAA released the footage with an official report in January 2017. Director Ricardo Bermúdez summarised the finding as 'We do not know what it was, but we do know what it was not.'

openQuestions: The full text of Resolución Exenta N° 01599 (3 October 1997) and Resolución Exenta N° 04/3/0113/1385 (18 October 2021) has not been located online; both are described in detail on DGAC and SEFAA pages but neither PDF is published there.
The DGAC page states CEFAA publishes resolved cases quarterly; Canada's 2025 report states SEFAA publishes monthly reports. Both are cited; the cadence may have changed after 2021.
CEFAA/SEFAA's annual budget and current headcount are not published.
The official CEFAA report on the 11 November 2014 Navy footage has not been retrieved in full; the characterisation above rests on press accounts of its release.

entities.label: SETKA-MO / SETKA-AN - USSR state programme on anomalous atmospheric and space phenomena, 1978-1990
entities.sub: The Soviet Union turned its entire army into a standing UAP sensor network for thirteen years, and then published
entities.locLabel: Moscow region, USSR (IZMIRAN; a central military research institute of the Ministry of Defence)
entities.desc:
SETKA is the largest state UAP data-collection effort ever run, and almost nothing about it looks like the American arrangement. It was created by a bureaucratic decision minuted at the Kremlin, funded out of nobody's budget, executed by fewer than a dozen people, mandated in writing to every Soviet serviceman, and - the part that matters here - written up afterwards by the two men who ran it and published in the Academy of Sciences' own journal.

The trigger was the Petrozavodsk phenomenon of 20 September 1977, a large-scale luminous event seen across the north-west USSR and into Finland by ambulance crews, militia, dockers, military personnel and airport staff, and reported in Izvestia three days later under the headline 'The Unidentified natural phenomenon'. Local authorities asked the Presidium of the Academy of Sciences to explain it; letters arrived from northern European governments asking whether the effects came from military-technical experiments and endangered the environment. Under that pressure the President of the Academy of Sciences, Academician Anatoly Aleksandrov, wrote to L. Smirnov, Vice-President of the government and Chairman of the Military-Industrial Commission, asking that a complex research programme on anomalous phenomena be started with Ministry of Defence and war-industry involvement. The MIC Scientific and Technical Council met in the Kremlin in October 1977 under Lieutenant-General B. A. Kijasov. Members noted that reports of extraordinary phenomena also reached Ministry of Defence organisations from servicemen, and had sometimes coincided with equipment failures.

The meeting recommended, and the MIC under the Council of Ministers adopted, the inclusion of two topics in the 1978 state plan of defence research: 'Setka MO' (Ministry of Defence) - 'Research of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena and their influence on the operation of military technical equipment and personnel' - and 'Setka AS' (Academy of Sciences) - 'Research of a physical nature and mechanisms of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena'. The programme ran without interruption for thirteen years, to 1990, and was re-approved in the five-year defence research plans of 1981 and 1986. Platov and Sokolov note that the October 1977 STC meeting 'was the first and last measure with a so high official level of the participants engaged in the problem'.

The execution was tiny. The military branch was led from one of the central military research institutes in the Moscow region, with its chief V. Balashov - an expert on radiation and other damaging factors on military equipment - as scientific head, and four to five specialists doing the collection, processing and analysis. Around fifteen further Ministry of Defence and war-industry organisations participated voluntarily and very limitedly. The academic branch was led by Academician V. Migulin, director of IZMIRAN, which was designated head institute; the working group there, also four to five people, was headed by Yu. Platov. Budget financing covered salaries and travel, drawn from the executing organisations' own budgets, with no special allocation - 'the most inexpensive one, if not the cheapest, among the scientific works on defensive subjects'.

The instrument that made it work was a document authorised by the Chief of the General Staff in January 1980 and distributed to the troops as a General Staff Directive. It designated the central military research institute as the collection, processing and analysis centre for all UAP information obtained by the military; named the research institutes responsible in all five arms; set the procedure by which the centre could obtain identification data, above all launch data for military aerospace systems; and fixed the rules for documenting detections and the reporting order by urgency. The authors' own summary is the sentence worth having verbatim: the directive 'for 13 years put the army into the on-duty regime of observation of the paranormal phenomena in the places of the army dislocation, i.e. practically on the whole territory of the USSR'. Every serviceman became, as they put it, 'without knowing it' a potential participant, obliged to report any inexplicable phenomenon in writing.

The work was classified for three stated reasons: it sat inside the classified defence research plan; a military-technical origin for the effects was thought likely at the outset; and there was a possible military application of properties such as absence of radar contrast and high manoeuvrability. The word 'UFO' was not used in official documents, which said 'anomalous phenomenon' instead - partly because it fitted the observations better, partly to keep clear of popular agitation about aliens arriving on flying saucers.

The results are what a large sensor network with a small analysis cell produces. Over thirteen years about three thousand messages arrived, describing more than 400 distinct events after mass-observation reports were consolidated. More than 90% were resolved as effects accompanying rocket and space launches - sunlight scattered off gas-and-dust clouds from rocket exhaust, visible over hundreds of kilometres in twilight geometry - or as high-altitude balloons, which accounted for 10-12% of messages. The Petrozavodsk event itself was attributed to the launch of Kosmos 955 from Plesetsk. Notably, reports did not come in from units at or near test ranges, where such effects were familiar. The 1984-87 series of flight emergencies at the Borisoglebsk air unit in Voronezh region, where unknown objects appeared on radar and were seen by pilots, the authors leave explicitly unidentified.

And then the finding that makes the programme worth a node rather than a footnote. Across thirteen years of compulsory reporting spanning roughly a sixth of the Earth's land surface, the programme received no report of a landing, no report of contact with occupants, and no report of an abduction. Platov and Sokolov put the conclusion as a fork: either the USSR was closed to alien visitation for at least thirteen years, or the extraterrestrial-origin hypothesis is inconsistent. They also dismiss the 1990s wave of claims about 'KGB secret files' and 'classified capture of UFO' as absurd. Whatever one makes of the conclusions, the contrast with the American record is the point: the Soviet state ran the collection openly enough inside its own system to mandate it army-wide, and its coordinators published the account under their own names in Vestnik Rossiiskoi Akademii Nauk in 2000.

claims.text: The Petrozavodsk phenomenon of 20 September 1977 was reported in Izvestia on 23 September 1977 under the title 'The Unidentified natural phenomenon', describing a 'huge "star" with impulsive beams of light coming to the ground' that hung over the town 'as a huge "jellyfish"'.
claims.source: Yu. V. Platov and B. A. Sokolov, translated from Vestnik Rossiiskoi Akademii Nauk, Vol. 70, No. 6, 2000, pp. 507-515 - http://www.debunker.com/historical/HistoryRussianUFOlogy.html

claims.text: Academy of Sciences President Anatoly Aleksandrov wrote to L. Smirnov, Vice-President of the government and Chairman of the Military-Industrial Commission, requesting urgent consideration of a complex research programme on anomalous phenomena involving Ministry of Defence and war-industry organisations.

The MIC Scientific and Technical Council met 'in October, 1977 in Kremlin under the presidency of general - lieutenant B.A.Kijasov'; members noted that reports of extraordinary phenomena also reached Ministry of Defence organisations from servicemen and that 'during such events sometimes were marked the cases of violation in the operation of the means of maintenance of the army forces'.

Two topics were entered in the 1978 defence research plan, verbatim: '"Setka MO" (Ministry of Defence) - "Research of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena and their influence on the operation of military technical equipment and personnel"; "Setka AS" (Academy of Sciences) - "Research of a physical nature and mechanisms of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena".'

'Thus, in 1978 in the USSR the state program of studying the "UFO" phenomenon started, and proceeded without interruption for 13 years down to 1990.' Five-year defence research plans including the anomalous-phenomena work were approved again in 1981 and 1986.

The military branch was led from 'one of the central military research institutes in the Moscow region', with its chief V. Balashov as scientific head and a working group of four to five people; roughly fifteen further Ministry of Defence and war-industry organisations participated voluntarily. The academic branch was headed by Academician V. Migulin, director of IZMIRAN, which was 'determined as the head institute in this field of activity', with a working group of four to five headed by Yu. Platov.

'The budget financing of the research program included the salary of the experts occupied in these activities and the costs of business trips. All the money was coming from the budget of organisations - executors and there was no special financing of the research.' The programme was 'the most inexpensive one, if not the cheapest, among the scientific works on defensive subjects'.

A document authorised by the Chief of the General Staff in January 1980 reached the troops as a General Staff Directive; it designated the central research institute as the collection, processing and analysis centre, named responsible institutes in all five arms, set the order for obtaining launch data needed for identification, and fixed rules for documenting and reporting detections by urgency.

Verbatim: 'One can say that the noted directive for 13 years put the army into the on-duty regime of observation of the paranormal phenomena in the places of the army dislocation, i.e. practically on the whole territory of the USSR, and this means, anyway, approximately 1/6 of the Earth territory.' Each serviceman 'became (without knowing it) a potential participant of the program'.

The research was classified for three stated reasons: it formally entered the classified defence plan; a military-technical origin for the effects was thought likely at the outset; and there was 'a capability of a military use of some probable properties of the UFO ... absence of a radar contrast, high manoeuvrability, etc.' In official documents 'the use of an abbreviation "UFO" was not accepted, instead of it the term "paranormal phenomenon" was used.'

'During the work on the program (for 13 years) about three thousand of messages reporting about extraordinary phenomena have been obtained ... on the whole, more than 400 events were registered and identified as extraordinary or paranormal.' Over 90% were resolved as rocket-launch effects or high-altitude balloons, the balloon class accounting for 10-12% of messages. The Petrozavodsk phenomenon itself was attributed to 'the launch of an artificial Earth satellite "Kosmos 955" from the space range in Plesetsk'. Reports 'did not practically come' from units at or near test ranges, where such effects were familiar.

Across the whole programme there was no message about a UFO landing, no message about contact with UFO occupants, and no message about abductions. The authors state the conclusion as a fork: 'either the territory of the USSR was, due to any reasons, closed for alien visitations during, at least, 13 years or that the hypothesis of an extraterrestrial origin of "UFO" is inconsistent.'

The series of flight emergencies in 1984-87 at the Borisoglebsk air unit in Voronezh region, characterised by unknown objects on radar and visually observed by pilots in emergency zones, is left explicitly unresolved: 'So far there is no consensus of opinion as to the role played in these emergencies by the mysterious objects observed in the zone of flight, and we shall interpret these events as unidentified.'
Secondary accounts state that the SETKA designations were changed to 'Galaktika' (MO and AN) in 1981 and to 'Gorizont' (MO and AN) in 1986.
claims.source: Paul Stonehill and Philip Mantle, 'Setka: A Secret Soviet UFO Research Program - Dawn of the Secret Program' - https://www.ufoinfo.com/news/setka.shtml

openQuestions: The Galaktika (1981) and Gorizont (1986) redesignations rest only on secondary ufological writing. Platov and Sokolov confirm that the five-year plans of 1981 and 1986 re-approved the work but do not name new codenames. The renaming is unverified from any primary or academic source.
The central Ministry of Defence research institute that led the military branch is not named in the published account, only located 'in the Moscow region'. Its identity is unestablished.
The January 1980 General Staff Directive itself has not been located in any archive or published facsimile; its contents are known only from Platov and Sokolov's description.
The archive of roughly 3,000 collected reports has not been shown to be publicly accessible. Unlike GEIPAN and SEFAA, this programme published a summary but not its case files.
The original Russian text in Vestnik Rossiiskoi Akademii Nauk has not been consulted; all quotations above are from the English translation supplied by James Oberg with the author's permission.
sources: Yu. V. Platov and B. A. Sokolov, 'Study of Unidentified Flying Objects in the Soviet Union', Vestnik Rossiiskoi Akademii Nauk, Vol. 70, No. 6, 2000, pp. 507-515 (English translation) - http://www.debunker.com/historical/HistoryRussianUFOlogy.html

edges.label: alleged crash site
edges.note: Scully's account placed the landing in Hart Canyon, roughly twelve miles northeast of the city of Aztec, San Juan County, New Mexico. The location is the only fixed and checkable element of the story, and it is the one the town later built a symposium and a commemorative plaque around.

edges.label: detail donor to later Roswell accounts
edges.note: After the story was revived in the 1970s, its specifics - small bodies, an intact hull, rapid military sanitisation of the site, storage at Wright-Patterson - migrated into allegedly first-hand Roswell testimony. A documented fraud became a supplier of narrative detail to the case the modern disclosure argument rests on, which is a contamination risk this board has to carry explicitly.
sources: John Michael Greer, 'The UFO Phenomenon: Fact, Fantasy and Disinformation', Llewellyn Worldwide, 2009, pp. 119ff - https://archive.org/details/ufophenomenonfac0000gree

edges.label: Air Force denials of Hangar 18 bodies
edges.note: Robert Spencer Carr's 1974 public claim that bodies recovered near Aztec were held at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson AFB drew official Air Force denials. The FBI separately disowned the Guy Hottel memo, the one federal document ever cited as corroboration, in a published 2013 statement.

edges.label: French national UAP office, CNES Toulouse
edges.note: GEIPAN is a technical department of CNES attached to the deputy directorate of the Toulouse Space Centre, with jurisdiction over sightings on French territory. CNES lists its location as Toulouse and its status as 'In operation' with an indefinite lifetime.

edges.label: shared IHEDN lineage; SEPRA head contributed
edges.note: COMETA's introduction states that GEPAN was created on the recommendations of a 1976 IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, and Jean-Jacques Velasco, then head of SEPRA at CNES, is named among the report's contributors. COMETA also recommended 'developing the actions of SEPRA'.

edges.label: French analysts worked the Chilean Navy FLIR case
edges.note: Photo and video analysts in France, including François Louange, were brought into CEFAA's investigation of the 11 November 2014 Chilean Navy infrared footage through GEIPAN. The two offices reached different conclusions - GEIPAN's analysts proposed a medium-haul aircraft venting, CEFAA rejected it - and both published. It is the clearest documented case of state UAP offices on two continents working the same tape.

edges.label: named as the model Canada should follow
edges.note: Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor examined GEIPAN in detail, told Canada that 'the example of GEIPAN in France is worth considering' when establishing a dedicated service, and recommended in recommendation 13 that Canada's lead organisation partner with 'AARO and NASA (U.S.A.), GEIPAN (France), and SEFAA (Chile)'.

edges.label: French private defence committee
edges.note: COMETA operated informally from 1996 and was registered as a non-profit association under the French law of 1901 on 24 February 1999; its membership was drawn almost entirely from French flag officers, weapons engineers and IHEDN auditors.

edges.label: IHEDN origin; delivered to the Prime Minister
edges.note: General Letty took the project to General Norlain at his IHEDN office in March 1995, and the report was subsequently delivered to the head of the French government. Robert Roussel, citing Jospin's chief of staff Olivier Schrameck, states the Prime Minister read and annotated it 'to mark his interest'. The handover route is not established from any primary document, hence tier 3.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COMETA_report citing Robert Roussel, 'Ovnis 1947-2017. Le choix du déni', L'Harmattan, 2018, p. 214

edges.label: adopts Hynek's Blue Book-era classification
edges.note: COMETA chapter 7.2 states that the strangest category D cases 'are generally labeled CE3s (close encounters of the third kind) according to the classification proposed by Professor A. Hynek, an astronomer and consultant to the USAF, within the context of the Blue Book Project'. Chapter 9 of the report separately surveys the organisation of research abroad.

edges.label: dedicated appendix on Roswell and disinformation
edges.note: COMETA's appendix 5 is titled 'The Roswell Affair - Disinformation'. A committee of retired French flag officers treating Roswell as a subject requiring an appendix in a defence study is itself part of what makes the document unusual.

edges.label: cites Soviet statistical distributions as comparable
edges.note: COMETA chapter 7.3 records that 'statistical studies in the USSR yielded distributions comparable to those determined by Claude Poher, the first head of GEPAN, from some 200 French cases, or 1,000 cases worldwide'. The report does not name SETKA, and the identification of the Soviet studies with the SETKA programme is inference rather than citation - hence tier 3.

edges.label: created and housed by the DGAC
edges.note: Created by DGAC Resolución Exenta N° 01599 of 3 October 1997, signed by Director General Gonzalo Miranda Aguirre; reorganised under the Secretaría General from 1 January 2010 by Resolución N° 02/0/01937; renamed SEFAA and moved under the Subdepartamento Comunicacional on 18 October 2021 by Resolución Exenta N° 04/3/0113/1385.

edges.label: sited in Santiago since 1997
edges.note: Established at the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in the Quinta Normal aeronautical complex, Santiago, the same site where Chile's 1968-1975 predecessor commission had operated out of the Oficina Meteorológica. SEFAA is now at Av. Pedro Aguirre Cerda 5100, Cerrillos, Santiago.

edges.label: named as one of three national models and a partner
edges.note: Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor identified the United States, France and Chile as the three national UAP reporting models worth examining, described SEFAA's operations and its commitment to transparency, and recommended Canada partner with SEFAA alongside AARO, NASA and GEIPAN.

edges.label: head institute of the Academy of Sciences branch
edges.note: Academician V. Migulin, director of IZMIRAN and a radio physicist specialising in oscillation theory, radio wave propagation and radiolocation, was made scientific head of the academic branch, and IZMIRAN was designated head institute. The four-to-five person working group there was headed by Yu. Platov, co-author of the programme's published account.

edges.label: run from Moscow: Kremlin decision, MoD institute, IZMIRAN
edges.note: The founding Scientific and Technical Council meeting of the Military-Industrial Commission was held in the Kremlin in October 1977; the lead military executor was 'one of the central military research institutes in the Moscow region'; and the academic branch was run from IZMIRAN, also in the Moscow region.

edges.label: opposite reporting posture: mandated versus stigmatised
edges.note: A January 1980 Directive of the Soviet General Staff obliged every serviceman to report any inexplicable phenomenon in writing and routed the results to a single analysis centre, putting the army 'into the on-duty regime of observation' for thirteen years. The contrast with the US chain of command over the same period, where reporting carried career risk and no service-wide collection mandate existed, is the comparison this node exists to make. The Soviet side of the comparison is documented by the programme's own coordinators; no institutional contact between the two is claimed.
